[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: English 'for each ...' or 'for 10 times' names a whole collection or a count to be handled at once, and a maths reading treats the header as simultaneous conditions. A Java for is a while loop in compact form: one init, then test-body-update repeated, one pass at a time.
[1] misconception (M) -> ForIsConditional: wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. Right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times.
[2] misconception (M) -> DoubleLoopIndexCount: wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
[3] misconception (M) -> ForWhileNotInterchangeable: wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. Right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.
[4] misconception (M) -> LoopHeaderIsEquations: wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.
[5] misconception (M) -> LoopCountIsStatementCount: wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. Right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.
[6] misconception (M) -> FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode: wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.
[7] misconception (M) -> ForLoopPartSkipped: wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.
[8] misconception (M) -> ForInitRepeats: wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. Right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test.
[9] misconception (M) -> ForUpdateBeforeBody: wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.
[10] misconception (M) -> LoopStepAlwaysOne: wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).
[11] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ForIsConditional: Applies the for sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on the first pass only, re-runs the init after a pass, or skips the test on some passes. (here mixing in: "The body of a for statement executes at most once")
[12] misconception (M) -> LoopImpliedByOneTest: wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.
[13] misconception (M) -> IdiomOverridesCode: wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
[14] misconception (M) -> ProgramEndsAfterLoop: wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

[0] names_the_element (N): The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Syntax: for (<initialize>; <boolean expression>; <increment>) { <statements> }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to <initialize>; while (<boolean expression>) { <statements> <increment>; }.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Run the initializer once; then repeatedly: test the condition (stop if false), execute the body, run the update.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A for statement has no value; the passes it makes are fixed by its header: for (int i = 1; i <= N; i++) sum += i; leaves sum = N(N+1)/2, and for (int i = 2; i <= 8; i += 2) prints 2, 4, 6, 8,.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One pass: the test reads the loop variable; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items.
[7] relation_to_neighbour (R): A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards; the flag must be declared before the loop.
[8] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: counted loop / counter-controlled repetition - do the body a known number of times, with the loop variable as a stepper (index, term number, trial number).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ForIsConditional: Rewriting a for as the equivalent while (init before, update at the end of the body) keeps behaviour, except that continue then skips the update and the loop variable stays in scope after the loop. Changing the bound or the step changes the pass count predictably (< to <= adds one pass).
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing for (int i = 0, i < n, i++): the compiler parses the commas as more declarators in the init and reports a syntax error.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after while (...) or for (...) is an empty statement that is the whole loop body; the block written next is not repeated. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: for (...); { body } runs the body once after the loop ends; while (cond); with a cond that the empty body cannot change hangs forever (infinite loop) when cond starts true.
[3] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use for when there is an initialization, an increment and a continuation test and the loop variable is not needed after the loop; use while when the loop variable is needed later or the number of passes depends on what happens in the body.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; right after if (...) is an empty statement that forms the whole then branch; the following statement or block is no longer part of the if. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any if (cond); followed by a statement or block: that statement runs for every input, whatever cond is (it compiles without error).
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The number of passes is fixed by the init, the test and the update together. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Wrong start value, < vs <=, a wrong step, or an extra update of the counter in the body (or outside the loop): the loop runs too few or too many passes (off by one, or skips values).
[6] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without braces, the body of an if, while or for is exactly one statement; indentation does not add statements to it. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A braceless header followed by two or more indented statements: only the first is controlled, the others run once, after the if/loop, on every input.
[7] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A variable declared in the for initializer exists only inside the for statement. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Reading i after for (int i = 0; ...) {...}: 'cannot find symbol'.

for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) gives i every valid index exactly once, in increasing order.
break leaves the for loop at once, without running the rest of the body or the remaining passes.
continue skips the rest of the loop body; in a for loop control goes straight to the increment statement and then the next test.
A fencepost loop is a for loop with one item handled outside it.
A flag search loop sets a boolean flag inside a loop when a pass finds the condition, and leaves it set afterwards.
A for loop whose condition never becomes false (or is left out) repeats forever unless a break ends it.
The statements in braces after the for header are the loop body; they run once on every pass, between the test and the increment, exactly as in a while loop.
A variable declared in the for header exists only from its declaration to the end of the for statement's block.
In nested loops the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
The simulation is a for loop over t = 0 ... T - 1 that makes one random move per pass.
The for header is exactly the three control slots, and the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass.
